title: The Most Boring Box in the World

bands.1:
I am a Bilbolster. I am a bilby with very big ears. Tonight, I am the one telling this story.

I live in a tiny cage in the Vantamart. The sign on my cage says, "LIVE MERCH." I wear a tiny gold hoodie. Every day, a Goldie takes my photo for Maxx's shop.

"Smile!" he says. I do not smile.

At nine o'clock, my big ears hear the back door.

"Fresh stock!" says a loud voice. "Everyone is ordering these! Sign here!"

"Why is that box breathing?" asks a Goldie.

"Deluxe model," says the voice.

Then the boxes walk in. They say, "LIFE-SIZED MAXX PILLOW." Out climb a crew of children and a man in a striped suit.

A quiet girl opens my cage. "You're safe," she whispers. Her name is Wren.

The crew goes into Maxx's office. A boy types IAMPRICELESS. The door opens.

Wren goes straight to a grey box. It says, "BORING STUFF. DO NOT OPEN."

"He hides the important things in boring boxes," she says.

Inside is a book. A girl called Tully reads it. "Money in: four million dollars. Money for Creatures: one carrot. Money for a second gold jet ski: all the rest!"

My ears stand straight up. That is proof.

"That's the proof," says the Captain.

Then the lights flash on. Goldies run in!

A boy called Gus throws a grey ball. "Fluff Bomb!" Smoke fills the room. It smells like an old jumper.

"Free hoodies at the front door!" shouts the man in the striped suit.

It is not true. My ears flop. But the Goldies run to the front anyway.

We run out the back. I do not go home. I hop into the Captain's bag.

On the boat, the Captain reads the last page of the book. "Biggest net ever. For THE BIG ONE."

What needs a net that big? My ears have never stood up so straight.
bands.2:
I am a Bilbolster: a bilby with ears so big they hear everything. Tonight, this is my story.

I live in a tiny cage at the back of the Vantamart. The sign says "LIVE MERCH". I wear a tiny gold hoodie, and every day a Goldie takes my photo for Maxx's catalogue.

"Smile for the Vantafam!" he says. I never smile.

Above the shelves, a billboard says, "EVERY DOLLAR GOES TO THE RESCUE FUND!" Every time I read it, my ears flop. Nothing holds that claim up.

At nine o'clock, my ears hear the back door open.

"Evening, gents! Fresh stock!" booms a voice. "Every shop on the planet is ordering these. Can you really afford NOT to sign?"

"Why is that box breathing?" asks a Goldie.

"Deluxe model," says the voice. "Comes with breathing."

A kookaburra cackles, "Koo-koo-ha-ha-HA!"

Soon the boxes walk into the studio. They say "LIFE-SIZED MAXX PILLOW". Out climb a crew of children in silver wigs and paper teeth, and a man in a striped suit.

A quiet girl kneels by my cage. "You're safe now," she whispers. The others call her Wren.

The crew stops at Maxx's office. A boy called Zed types IAMPRICELESS, and the door swings open.

Wren walks past every box to a grey one on the bottom shelf: "BORING STUFF. DO NOT OPEN."

"He always hides important things in a boring box," she says, very quietly.

Inside is the Rescue Fund ledger. Tully reads it. "Money in, from hoodies: four million dollars. Money spent on Creatures: one carrot. The rest went on a second gold jet ski!"

My ears shoot straight up. That is a claim with proof.

"That's the proof," says the Captain, and tucks the ledger away.

Then the lights snap on, and Goldies pour in.

Gus bowls a grey ball down the aisle. Thick smoke billows out, smelling of old jumper. "Belly-button fluff," he says proudly. "Two years of it."

The man in the striped suit jumps onto a shelf. "Free gold hoodies at the front door! Everybody's getting one!"

There are no free hoodies. My ears flop. But every Goldie stampedes to the front.

We slip out the back. The other Creatures scamper off into the red dust. I do not. I hop into the Captain's bag.

On the boat, the Captain reads the last page of the ledger aloud. "Biggest net ever made. Paid for by the Vantafam. For THE BIG ONE."

"Nobody needs a net that big," says the man in the striped suit.

Somebody does. My ears have never stood up so straight.
bands.3:
I am a Bilbolster, a bilby with ears so big they hear every word in the building. Tonight, for once, I get to tell the story.

I live in a cage at the back of the Vantamart, in a row of cages labelled "LIVE MERCH". I wear a tiny gold hoodie that is two sizes too small. Every morning a Goldie sits us in front of a gold backdrop and takes photos for Maxx's catalogue.

"Smile for the Vantafam!" he says. I have never smiled once.

Above the shelves hangs a billboard: "EVERY DOLLAR GOES TO THE RESCUE FUND!" Every time I read it, my ears flop. A claim with nothing holding it up does that to them.

At nine o'clock, my ears pick up the back door rolling open.

"Evening, gents! Fresh stock!" booms a voice like a market stall. "Every shop on the planet is ordering these. Can you really afford NOT to sign?"

"Why is that one breathing?" asks a Goldie.

"Deluxe model. Comes with breathing."

A kookaburra cackles, "Koo-koo-ha-ha-HA!" and the Goldies laugh along and wave the boxes through.

A few minutes later, the boxes walk into our studio. Each one is stamped "LIFE-SIZED MAXX PILLOW". Out climb a crew of children in gold tracksuits, steel-wool wigs and paper teeth, followed by a man in a red-and-white striped suit.

The Puffentie in the end cage hears one of them whisper "rescued", puffs up in fury and bursts his hoodie. A quiet girl kneels by my cage and works the lock. "You're safe now," she whispers. The others call her Wren.

The crew stops at Maxx's office. A boy called Zed tries MAXXISGREAT, then IAMPRICELESS, and the door swings open. "That's not a password," he mutters. "That's a cry for help."

Wren walks past every filing box to a dusty grey one on the bottom shelf: "BORING STUFF. DO NOT OPEN."

"He always hides the important things in a boring box," she says, so quietly that only the Captain and I hear.

Inside is the Rescue Fund ledger. A girl called Tully runs her finger down it. "Money in, from hoodies: four million dollars. Money spent on Creatures: one carrot. Money spent on a second gold jet ski, 'for Sundays': everything else."

My ears shoot straight up. That claim has proof under it.

"That's the proof," says the Captain, and slips the ledger inside a jacket.

Then the lights snap on, and Goldies pour in from the loading dock. "Pillows don't have legs!" one yells.

Gus bowls a lumpy grey ball down the aisle. Thick smoke billows out, smelling of old jumper. "Belly-button fluff," he says proudly. "Two years of it."

The striped man leaps onto a shelf. "Roll up, roll up! Free gold hoodies at the front door! Everybody's getting one!"

There are no free hoodies. My ears flop flat. But every Goldie in the building stampedes to the front.

We slip out the back. The others scamper off into the red dust in their tiny hoodies. I do not. I hop into the Captain's bag.

On the boat, the Captain reads the last page of the ledger aloud: "Biggest net ever made. Paid for by the Vantafam. For THE BIG ONE."

"I've sold a lot of nets," says the striped man quietly. "Nobody needs one that big."

Somebody does, and the Vantafam paid for it. My ears have never stood up so straight.
bands.4:
I am a Bilbolster, a bilby whose ears are so large that, on a quiet night, I can hear a Goldie decide what to have for lunch. Nobody has ever asked me to tell a story. Tonight, nobody needs to.

My cage is the third in a row at the back of the Vantamart, under a sign that says "LIVE MERCH". I wear a gold hoodie two sizes too small, with a hood that folds my ears in half. Every morning, a Goldie lines us up in front of a gold backdrop and photographs us for Maxx's catalogue, and every morning he says the same thing.

"Smile for the Vantafam!"

I have not smiled once. I am not sure bilbies can, and I am quite sure I would not.

Above the shelves hangs a billboard: "EVERY DOLLAR GOES TO THE RESCUE FUND!" Whenever I read it, my ears flop. They always do that when a claim has nothing underneath it, the way a tent sags when someone has forgotten the poles.

At nine o'clock, the back door rolls open, and a voice like a whole market booms in.

"Evening, gents! Fresh stock! Every shop on the planet is ordering these. Can you really afford NOT to sign?"

Three claims, no poles. My ears are already halfway down.

"Why is that one breathing?" asks a Goldie.

"Deluxe model," says the voice, without missing a beat. "Comes with breathing."

Somewhere above the voice, a kookaburra cackles, and the Goldies, who have clearly never heard of a kookaburra laughing at a lie, laugh along and wave the boxes through.

Ten minutes later, the boxes walk into our studio. Each is stamped "LIFE-SIZED MAXX PILLOW", and out of each climbs a child in a gold tracksuit, a steel-wool wig and a set of paper teeth painted so white they hurt. Last of all comes the owner of the voice: a man in a red-and-white striped suit, his moustache waxed into two neat curls.

The Puffentie in the end cage hears one of them whisper "rescued". He has heard that word before, on Maxx's streams, so he puffs up to twice his size and bursts his hoodie at every seam.

A small, quiet girl kneels in front of my cage. She does not say "rescued". She works the lock with steady fingers and says, "There you go," which I find I believe completely.

The crew stops at the office door. The gamer one tries MAXXISGREAT, frowns, then types IAMPRICELESS, and the door swings open. "That's not a password," he mutters. "That's a cry for help."

Inside, the quiet girl walks past every filing box in the room, as if she knows the way, and stops at a dusty grey one on the bottom shelf: "BORING STUFF. DO NOT OPEN. SERIOUSLY, IT'S SO BORING."

"He always hides the important things in a boring box," she says, so softly that only the Captain and I hear it.

Inside is a fat gold book, the Rescue Fund ledger. The one who counts everything runs her finger down its columns. "Money in, from hoodies: four million dollars. Money spent on Creatures: one carrot. Money spent on a second gold jet ski, 'for Sundays': everything else."

My ears rise so fast that the hood splits.

The Captain tucks the ledger inside a jacket, says nothing at all, and nods at the door.

Then the lights snap on. Goldies pour in from the loading dock, and one of them, who is cleverer than he looks, shouts, "Pillows don't have legs!"

The engineer bowls a lumpy grey ball down the aisle. It smokes, thickly, and smells of every old jumper I have ever been squashed against. In the fog, the striped man leaps onto a shelf and cups his hands round his mouth.

"ROLL UP, ROLL UP! Free gold hoodies at the front door! Everybody's getting one!"

There are no free hoodies. My ears could not be flatter. Every Goldie in the building runs for the front door anyway, and I learn something about claims that nobody had ever taught me: a lie with no poles can still move a crowd.

We slip out the back. On the dock, the other Creatures scamper off into the red dust, still in their hoodies. I do not. I climb into the Captain's bag, and nobody tells me to get out.

On the Soggy Biscuit, the Captain turns to the last page of the ledger and reads it aloud: "Biggest net ever made. Paid for by the Vantafam. For THE BIG ONE."

"Friends," says the striped man, "I've sold a lot of nets. Nobody needs one that big."

Nobody answers him. Out past the boat, the sea is black and very wide, and the Vantafam have already paid for whatever Maxx means to pull out of it.

My ears, for the record, are standing straight up.
